title: Fronting, information structure and focus
objectives: Identify the function of fronting in context.
Form object fronting without repeating the object.
Distinguish ordinary order from negative and locative inversion.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: Fronting places an element near the beginning of a clause instead of its more usual position. It can connect a sentence to material already mentioned, establish a frame, or make a contrast prominent. Compare “The first proposal we can accept; the second needs more work” with “We can accept the first proposal, but the second needs more work.” The fronted object makes the contrast between the proposals easy to follow.

English does not front every element equally naturally. A sentence can be grammatical yet sound marked or awkward without a suitable context. In speech, intonation also helps listeners recognise the contrast; in writing, punctuation and surrounding sentences provide clues.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: A fronted object normally leaves the subject and verb in their regular order: “That question we can answer later.” Do not normally repeat the object with a pronoun: “That question we can answer”, not “That question we can answer it”, in standard written English. A fronted time or place phrase also usually precedes normal subject–verb order: “After the meeting, the team reviewed the notes.”

Some place expressions can be followed by full inversion, especially in literary descriptions: “On the hill stood an old tower.” Here the main verb stood precedes the noun phrase subject. This pattern differs from negative-expression inversion such as “Rarely had she visited”: in the latter an auxiliary precedes the subject.

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Imagine an editor reviewing two chapters: “The first chapter we can publish now. The second needs revision.” Fronting the first object links the sentence to the comparison already under discussion. In a report, “As for the budget, we need another estimate” explicitly introduces a topic before commenting on it. A topic tells readers what the clause is about; the focus is the information made prominent in a particular context.

In a descriptive passage, “Across the valley lay a small village” places a setting before the item introduced into the scene. Compare the neutral “A small village lay across the valley.” The fronted version may support the flow of a scene, but it can be too literary for routine instructions.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Fronting a place phrase does not require inversion in every sentence: “In the garden, the children played” is natural. The fully inverted “In the garden played the children” is more restricted and would often sound literary or awkward in ordinary conversation. Pronoun subjects also favour ordinary order in many such contexts: “Here she comes” rather than “Here comes she”.

Do not confuse a fronted object with a fronted negative expression. “This result we had expected” keeps the subject before had; “Never had we expected this result” puts had before the subject. Choose the structure according to the element fronted, its meaning and the intended register.

common_errors.incorrect: That question we can answer it later.
common_errors.correct: That question we can answer later.
common_errors.reason: Do not repeat the fronted object with it in this standard written pattern.

common_errors.correct: After the meeting, the team reviewed the notes.
common_errors.reason: The fronted time phrase normally takes ordinary subject–verb order.

common_errors.correct: Never had we expected this result.

summary: Fronting can establish a topic, frame a clause or highlight a contrast.
A fronted object normally leaves the subject and verb in regular order.
Some place expressions permit full inversion, often with a literary effect.

exercises.prompt: Two proposals are being contrasted. Which sentence fronts the object?
exercises.explanation: The first proposal is the object placed before the subject we.

options.text: The first proposal we can accept.
We can accept the first proposal.

option_feedback.a: “The first proposal we can accept.” fits here. The first proposal is the object placed before the subject we.
option_feedback.b: “We can accept the first proposal.” does not fit here. The first proposal is the object placed before the subject we.
option_feedback.c: “The first proposal is acceptable.” does not fit here. The first proposal is the object placed before the subject we.
option_feedback.d: “We accept the proposal first.” does not fit here. The first proposal is the object placed before the subject we.

exercises.prompt: Complete the standard written pattern: That question ___.
exercises.explanation: The fronted object is not repeated; the subject precedes can.

option_feedback.a: “we can answer it later” does not fit here. The fronted object is not repeated; the subject precedes can.
option_feedback.b: “can we answer it later” does not fit here. The fronted object is not repeated; the subject precedes can.
option_feedback.c: “we can answer later” fits here. The fronted object is not repeated; the subject precedes can.
option_feedback.d: “we later can it answer” does not fit here. The fronted object is not repeated; the subject precedes can.

exercises.prompt: Choose normal order after a fronted time phrase.
exercises.explanation: A fronted time phrase normally leaves subject–verb order unchanged.

options.text: After lunch reviewed the team the notes.
After lunch the team did reviewed the notes.
After lunch did reviewed the team the notes.
After lunch, the team reviewed the notes.

option_feedback.a: “After lunch reviewed the team the notes.” does not fit here. A fronted time phrase normally leaves subject–verb order unchanged.
option_feedback.b: “After lunch the team did reviewed the notes.” does not fit here. A fronted time phrase normally leaves subject–verb order unchanged.
option_feedback.c: “After lunch did reviewed the team the notes.” does not fit here. A fronted time phrase normally leaves subject–verb order unchanged.
option_feedback.d: “After lunch, the team reviewed the notes.” fits here. A fronted time phrase normally leaves subject–verb order unchanged.

exercises.prompt: Choose the literary locative inversion.
exercises.explanation: Stood precedes the noun subject after the place phrase.

options.text: On the hill an old tower stood it.
On the hill stood an old tower.
On the hill did stood an old tower.
On the hill an old tower did stood.

option_feedback.a: “On the hill an old tower stood it.” does not fit here. Stood precedes the noun subject after the place phrase.
option_feedback.b: “On the hill stood an old tower.” fits here. Stood precedes the noun subject after the place phrase.
option_feedback.c: “On the hill did stood an old tower.” does not fit here. Stood precedes the noun subject after the place phrase.
option_feedback.d: “On the hill an old tower did stood.” does not fit here. Stood precedes the noun subject after the place phrase.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses the usual pronoun order?
exercises.explanation: The pronoun subject she normally precedes comes.

option_feedback.a: “Here comes she.” does not fit here. The pronoun subject she normally precedes comes.
option_feedback.b: “Here does comes she.” does not fit here. The pronoun subject she normally precedes comes.
option_feedback.c: “Here she come does.” does not fit here. The pronoun subject she normally precedes comes.
option_feedback.d: “Here she comes.” fits here. The pronoun subject she normally precedes comes.

exercises.prompt: In “As for the budget, we need an estimate”, what is introduced first?
exercises.explanation: As for the budget introduces the topic.

option_feedback.a: “The main verb.” does not fit here. As for the budget introduces the topic.
option_feedback.b: “The topic of the comment.” fits here. As for the budget introduces the topic.
option_feedback.c: “The direct object of estimate.” does not fit here. As for the budget introduces the topic.
option_feedback.d: “A past obligation.” does not fit here. As for the budget introduces the topic.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence uses negative-expression inversion?
exercises.explanation: Initial never puts the auxiliary had before the subject.

options.text: Never had we expected the delay.
The report we can read later.

option_feedback.a: “The delay we had expected.” does not fit here. Initial never puts the auxiliary had before the subject.
option_feedback.b: “After lunch we left.” does not fit here. Initial never puts the auxiliary had before the subject.
option_feedback.c: “Never had we expected the delay.” fits here. Initial never puts the auxiliary had before the subject.
option_feedback.d: “The report we can read later.” does not fit here. Initial never puts the auxiliary had before the subject.

exercises.prompt: What is a likely effect of repeated literary fronting in routine instructions?
exercises.explanation: Marked fronting can sound too literary for routine instructions.

options.text: It may make the register unnecessarily elaborate.

option_feedback.a: “It may make the register unnecessarily elaborate.” fits here. Marked fronting can sound too literary for routine instructions.
option_feedback.b: “It always makes them shorter.” does not fit here. Marked fronting can sound too literary for routine instructions.
option_feedback.c: “It is required for correctness.” does not fit here. Marked fronting can sound too literary for routine instructions.
option_feedback.d: “It removes all ambiguity.” does not fit here. Marked fronting can sound too literary for routine instructions.

exercises.explanation: Initial never triggers auxiliary–subject inversion.

exercises.explanation: A fronted place phrase does not require inversion.
